newsitem.title: FRANCE: Prices buoyant at French Burgundy charity auction.
newsitem.headline: Prices buoyant at French Burgundy charity auction.

text.p: Burgundy wine prices were buoyant at the annual Hospices de Beaune charity auction on Sunday, supported by what experts called the high quality of the ample 1996 vintage.
Prices for the 607 casks of red wine and 112 of white on offer were up on average 11.9 percent over last year's sale.
Ahead of the sale, trade specialists had predicted increases of 10 to 20 percent. In 1995, prices rose 7.8 percent on average after soaring by more than 50 percent in 1994.
The auction, closely watched in wine circles around the world, provides a barometer of prices and the overall health of France's important wine trade.
But Burgundy Wine Board officials cautioned that consumers should not necessarily expect prices in wine shops to follow the trend set at the Beaune auction.

The white wine fetching the highest price at this year's auction was a Batard-Montrachet "Dames de Flandres". Four barrels of 228 litres (just over 50 gallons) sold for 82,500 francs ($16,175) each, which was 41 percent less than they cost in 1995.
The dearest red this year was the Clos de la Roche "Cyrot-Chaudron", three barrels of which went for 57,000 francs ($11,176) each. That was eight percent more than last year.
The auction provided the earliest assessment of the market for the 1996 vintage, which was harvested just two months ago.

The wine-drinking public will have their first chance to sample the new vintage on Thursday, when bottles of Beaujolais Nouveau from a region at the southern end of Burgundy are uncorked around the world amid much hype and celebration.
Sale proceeds were 18.4 million francs ($3.6 million), which will be donated to Beaune's charity hospital after production costs are deducted.
Wine Board officials, who had pleaded publicly before Sunday's auction for moderation at the sale, said they were pleased with the sale's success but would have preferred greater price stability.
"The best thing for Burgundy and wine drinkers would be for great wine to be sold at stable prices," said Louis Trebuchet, Burgundy wine board president.

"We want a better link between quality and price," he said, explaining that Burgundy's international reputation for sky-high prices and variable quality could be improved if prices remained less volatile in the years ahead.
Wine professionals said that cool, wet conditions in July and August combined with excellent weather during the harvest would produce wines with the greatest potential for some time.
"It's the best year since 1990," said one trade journalist with 15 years' experience tasting the young wine out of huge oak barrels.
Trebuchet was more expansive, saying he believed the region had not produced such quantity with such consistent quality since 1959.

Average yields this year were about 30 percent higher than in 1995. But despite the increase, alcohol and acidity levels were high, color robust and tannins evident, indicating good potential for ageing, professionals said.

Proceeds from the auction after production costs go to the Hospices, built in 1443 by a tax collector for the king who, local legend has it, wanted to make up for some of his harsh tax-collecting practices over the years.
The traditional auction dates from 1859 and has been held every third Sunday in November since 1924.
